strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing visual token computation and KV-cache memory in MLLM inference, especially for high-resolution image and video inputs.

The proposed ZipR1 idea is simple and deployment-oriented: post-train an existing sparse-attention MLLM using a reward that combines answer correctness with token reduction, rather than requiring full pretraining or a new architecture.

The empirical tables cover multiple Qwen2/Qwen2.5-VL model sizes and a reasonably broad set of 13 image/video benchmarks, and the reported token-ratio reductions relative to ZipVL are large while benchmark scores are mostly preserved.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not sufficient to support the central efficiency claim. The paper reports token ratios but no wall-clock latency, throughput, GPU memory, KV-cache size, or hardware-specific inference measurements. For an efficiency paper, this is a major omission.

Novelty is limited. ZipR1 appears to combine an existing sparse-attention method, ZipVL, with a fairly standard GRPO-style reward over accuracy and sparsity. The paper does not clearly distinguish what is technically new beyond this straightforward reward formulation.

The experimental comparison is narrow: baselines are essentially Full and ZipVL. There are no comparisons to other token pruning, sparse attention, or adaptive inference methods, and no evidence that RL is better than simpler alternatives such as supervised fine-tuning, threshold tuning, or direct sparsity regularization.

Important training and reproducibility details are missing or unclear, including RL hyperparameters, number of samples per group, training compute, dataset splits, answer-matching procedure, reward scaling, KL coefficient, batch sizes, number of updates, and whether any benchmark data may overlap with Video-R1-260k.

There are no ablations isolating the effects of the performance reward, efficiency reward, KL term, random threshold sampling, choice of p range, or ZipVL backbone. This makes it difficult to know why the method works or whether the claimed design choices matter.

The method description has technical ambiguities and possible inconsistencies. For example, the sparse attention equations describe zeroing Q/K rather than masking logits, which would not necessarily remove attention to unselected tokens; the text says thresholds are sampled from U(0,1), while experiments use p in [0.94, 0.975].

The claimed minimal degradation is somewhat overstated: some benchmarks do drop, and no statistical variance or significance analysis is provided. Several improvements over Full attention are surprising and unexplained, raising questions about evaluation noise.

The paper is very short and underdeveloped for a top-tier submission: related work positioning is thin, there is little analysis of failure cases or qualitative behavior, and the conclusion repeats the abstract rather than synthesizing evidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing visual token computation and KV-cache cost in MLLMs without large drops in benchmark accuracy.
The proposed framing of token sparsity as an inference-aligned post-training objective is simple and potentially useful, especially if it can be made robust across sparsity levels.
The evaluation covers multiple Qwen2/Qwen2.5-VL model sizes and a reasonably broad set of image and video benchmarks, and the reported token-ratio reductions are large relative to the ZipVL baseline.
weaknesses: The technical formulation has serious soundness issues. The sparse attention equation appears to zero Q/K rows rather than masking logits, and V is not masked in the attention output, so the written mechanism does not actually exclude pruned tokens in the usual sense. The token-budget definition is also confusing and may not correspond cleanly to the reported token ratios.

The main efficiency claim is not directly evaluated. The paper reports token ratios but gives no wall-clock latency, prefill speed, decoding speed, memory usage, KV-cache size, throughput, or hardware-specific measurements. For an inference acceleration paper, this is a major missing piece.

The RL method is underspecified. Important details such as trainable parameters, number of samples, optimizer, learning rate, training steps, batch size, KL coefficient, clipping value, reward scaling, exact answer-matching rule, and compute budget are missing, making the method hard to reproduce.

There is an inconsistency between the method section, which says thresholds are sampled from U(0,1), and the experimental setup, which says p is in [0.94, 0.975]. This matters because exploration over sparsity levels is central to the claimed contribution.

The evaluation is too narrow in baselines and ablations. The paper compares only Full, ZipVL, and ZipR1, without comparisons to other sparse attention/token pruning methods or ablations isolating the performance reward, efficiency reward, KL term, threshold sampling, and calibration data.

The reported accuracy differences are often very small and sometimes positive despite aggressive pruning, but no variance, confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance analysis is provided. It is difficult to tell whether the changes are meaningful or just evaluation noise.

The paper does not establish that ZipR1 learns a better sparsity-performance frontier. Results are shown only at one inference setting, with no curves across token budgets and no analysis of whether the same accuracy could be obtained by simply tuning ZipVL's threshold.

The novelty appears limited: the contribution is essentially applying a GRPO-style reward to an existing sparse attention method, and the paper does not provide enough conceptual or empirical evidence that this is a substantial advance over threshold tuning or supervised/distillation-based calibration.

The presentation is quite thin for a top-tier venue. There are typos and imprecise phrases, the objective is written unclearly, the experimental section is very short, and important implementation and evaluation details are absent.

Potential data contamination or benchmark leakage is not discussed despite using a large Video-R1 calibration dataset and evaluating on many popular image/video benchmarks. The paper also gives no release plan for code, trained checkpoints, or processed data.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the inference cost of multimodal LLMs, especially for high-resolution image and video inputs where visual tokens dominate prefill and KV-cache costs.

The proposed ZipR1 framework is simple and appealing: it uses RL post-training to directly reward both answer correctness and token sparsity, making the optimization objective better aligned with the sparse-attention inference setting than ordinary supervised finetuning.

The empirical token reduction is substantial. Across Qwen2/Qwen2.5 VL models and 13 image/video benchmarks, the reported token ratio drops from roughly 70-80% under ZipVL to about 21-24% under ZipR1, with generally small accuracy degradation.
The evaluation spans multiple model sizes and both image and video benchmarks, which provides useful evidence that the method is not narrowly tuned to a single dataset or architecture variant.
The method is built on top of an existing sparse attention system, ZipVL, making the contribution practically relevant as a post-training enhancement rather than a complete architectural replacement.
weaknesses: The paper relies almost entirely on token ratio as the efficiency metric. For an inference-efficiency paper, the absence of measured wall-clock latency, throughput, peak memory, and KV-cache memory savings is a major limitation, especially because token sparsity does not always translate cleanly into realized acceleration.

The baseline set is too narrow. The main comparison is Full attention versus ZipVL versus ZipR1; the paper does not compare against other recent sparse attention or token pruning approaches under matched settings, making it hard to judge competitiveness beyond improving ZipVL.

Ablations are largely missing. The paper should isolate the contributions of the performance reward, efficiency reward, KL term, random p sampling, reward weighting, and choice of sparse attention backend. Without these, the source of the gains is underdetermined.

Training and reproducibility details are insufficient for a top-tier submission. Important information such as training budget, number of RL steps, batch/group size, learning rate, KL coefficient, reward implementation, hardware, data filtering, and exact post-training protocol is not clearly reported.

Some methodological details are confusing or potentially inconsistent. The method says p is sampled from U(0,1), while the experimental setup says p is set in [0.94, 0.975] with step 0.005, and inference uses p=0.975. This needs clarification because it affects both exploration and the reported sparsity behavior.

The results show impressive compression but mixed task performance: many numbers are slightly below full attention, and the paper does not report averages, confidence intervals, statistical variance, or significance tests. The claim of minimal degradation is plausible but not rigorously quantified.

The formulation of sparse attention and token budget could be clearer. For example, the definition of b using masks and d is awkward, and the sparse attention equation appears to mask Q and K but not explicitly V in the attention output, while later text discusses pruning KV cache. This may be a presentation issue, but it weakens technical clarity.

The paper is quite short and underspecified relative to the strength of its claims. It would benefit from deeper analysis of failure cases, sensitivity to target sparsity, per-layer/token behavior, and whether the learned model generalizes to out-of-domain prompts or longer videos.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: reducing visual token cost for MLLM inference, especially for high-resolution images and long videos, where KV-cache and prefill costs are major deployment bottlenecks.

The proposed idea of treating token reduction as an explicit reward in an inference-aligned GRPO post-training loop is conceptually clean and better aligned with deployment than proxy attention-sharpness objectives.
Empirical results are broad: the paper evaluates multiple Qwen2/Qwen2.5-VL and LLaVA-Video backbones across 13 image/video benchmarks, plus HallusionBench and latency/memory measurements.

The reported efficiency-accuracy trade-off is strong if reproducible: roughly 23-30% retained tokens with near-full-model accuracy across many tasks, and notable speed/memory gains at long sequence lengths.
The paper includes useful ablations over sparse attention mechanism, budget range, group size, and qualitative/quantitative evidence that training changes token sparsity patterns.
weaknesses: A key missing ablation is disentangling sparsity forcing from general RL/task tuning. The method trains on Video-R1/LLaVA-Video data, but there is no full-attention or ZipVL-only GRPO/SFT control using the same training data, so some accuracy preservation or gains may come from additional task adaptation rather than the proposed efficiency reward.

The reward and correctness computation are underspecified for open-ended multimodal benchmarks. Binary correctness is easy for some multiple-choice tasks but much less clear for OCR, chart QA, caption-like, or video tasks; reproducibility depends heavily on these details.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. MOBA, sharpness loss, FastV, VisionZip, Minference, and ZipVL differ in implementation assumptions, training budgets, and target ratios. The post-training baselines appear relatively weak, and some are not evaluated across all models/tasks.

Several important ablations are absent: performance-only reward, efficiency-only reward, no group normalization, no KL, fixed-budget rollouts, different inference p values after training, and training cost versus inference savings break-even analysis.

The method section has notation and clarity issues. For example, Eq. 5 overloads p as both threshold and integer token count, and the KL/reference-policy formulation is unclear when the policy uses sparse attention and the reference uses full causal attention.

Runtime claims need more detail. The comparison to FlashAttention-2 and ZipVL should specify hardware, batch size, generation length, implementation maturity, prefill/decoding split, and whether sparse indexing overhead is included end to end.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper lacks training steps, batch sizes, rollout sampling details, decoding parameters, exact data filtering, benchmark prompts, evaluator settings, and whether code/models will be released.

The paper makes strong general claims about explicitly reinforcing sparsity, but the implementation is built mainly on ZipVL/top-p pruning; it is not yet clear how broadly the method transfers to other sparse attention mechanisms beyond small ablations.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the visual-token/KV-cache burden of MLLMs for high-resolution image and long-video inference.
The proposed idea of using multi-budget rollouts and a joint accuracy-efficiency reward is conceptually appealing and reasonably aligned with deployment-time sparse inference.
The empirical section covers many image and video benchmarks and several backbones, and the headline results suggest large token-ratio reductions with little average accuracy loss.
The paper includes some useful ablations on sparse attention choices, budget ranges, group sizes, hallucination sensitivity, and runtime/memory scaling.
weaknesses: The core optimization story is not technically convincing. The sampled sparsity threshold appears to be an external variable rather than an action with a modeled probability, yet the GRPO objective is written over answer likelihoods. It is unclear how the RL update actually learns a budget/pruning policy rather than merely fine-tuning answer generation under randomly imposed masks.

Several method definitions are imprecise or inconsistent. For example, Eq. 5 reuses p as both threshold and token count, the sparse attention formulation masks Q/K but not V, and the claimed approximation bound is not sufficiently derived or connected to the implemented ZipVL-style pruning.

The reward and training setup are under-specified. The paper does not clearly explain how correctness rewards are computed for diverse open-ended multimodal tasks during training, what labels/evaluators are used, whether reward leakage from benchmark-style data is avoided, or how noisy binary rewards are handled.

The evaluation is not strong enough to support the main claims. There are no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or statistical tests, despite many gains being tiny and sometimes within likely benchmark noise. Some results even slightly exceed the full-attention model, which needs much more careful analysis.

Baselines are not sufficiently fair or complete. The strongest comparison should include budget-matched and tuned versions of ZipVL/FastV/VisionZip/MInference, not only their default token ratios. The post-training baselines such as MOBA and sharpness loss are weakly described and may not be appropriate or well-tuned for MLLMs.

Runtime comparisons are not adequately specified and are partly unfair. Comparing against dense FlashAttention-2 at very long contexts establishes that sparsity can help, but does not isolate the benefit of the proposed RL training over existing sparse implementations under identical kernels, hardware, batch sizes, sequence lengths, and generation settings.

The paper claims flexible budget control, but the implementation section says inference simply fixes p=0.975. This weakens the claim that the learned method provides an adaptive inference-time policy.

Reproducibility is limited. Important details are missing, including training steps, number of samples, exact rollout procedure, prompt/evaluation templates, reward implementation, benchmark preprocessing, train/eval data overlap checks, and code availability.
The average metrics combine heterogeneous benchmark scales such as MME/OCRBench point scores and percentage accuracies, making the reported averages difficult to interpret and potentially misleading.

Overall, while the direction is interesting, the paper currently has major unresolved issues in technical soundness, experimental rigor, and clarity. I would not consider it competitive for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference in its current form.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: reducing visual token computation and KV-cache cost for MLLM inference while preserving accuracy.

The core idea is clear and appealing: use grouped multi-budget rollouts with a joint correctness/efficiency reward so that sparsity is optimized in an inference-aligned way rather than through an attention-sharpness proxy.

Empirical results are broad, covering 13 image and video benchmarks across Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and LLaVA-Video backbones, with consistently large token-ratio reductions and small reported accuracy drops.

The paper includes useful comparisons against training-free sparse methods such as FastV, VisionZip, ZipVL, and MInference, plus post-training baselines such as MOBA-style sparse attention and sharpness regularization.
Runtime and memory measurements strengthen the practical relevance, especially the reported gains at long sequence lengths.

Ablations over sparse attention type, budget range, group size, low-budget behavior, hallucination sensitivity, and context length help support the central claim that learned sparsity remains controllable and robust.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental: the method largely combines an existing sparse attention mechanism with GRPO-style relative rewards, and the conceptual advance over reward-tuning an efficiency objective is not deeply analyzed.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. Important training information such as number of optimization steps, batch size, rollout group size used in main experiments, exact reward/evaluation matching rules, prompt formats, data filtering, and implementation details for sparse KV-cache handling are not sufficiently specified.

The binary correctness reward is underspecified for heterogeneous open-ended multimodal tasks. It is unclear how correctness is computed during training, whether learned/evaluator-based rewards are used, and how noisy reward signals affect optimization.

The fairness of the post-training baselines is not fully convincing. MOBA and sharpness-loss adaptations may be disadvantaged if not carefully tuned for MLLMs, and the paper provides limited hyperparameter or compute matching evidence.
Potential train-test contamination or benchmark proximity is not discussed, especially because Video-R1-260k and LLaVA-Video data are used for calibration while many public benchmarks are evaluated.

The runtime comparison needs more detail: hardware, batch size, kernel implementation, prefill versus decode decomposition, and whether all baselines use equally optimized sparse kernels are not fully clear.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, the paper claims direct end-to-end control and general deployment alignment, but most evidence is on a small family of sparse mechanisms and model families.

The mathematical presentation has several notation issues, including overloaded use of p in top-p thresholding and Eq. 5, and the sparse attention formulation is simplified relative to actual causal/multimodal attention behavior.
